label: cor:four-descendants
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Propagation from one level to the next

title: Proof
body_md:
The lower branch is Corollary~\ref{thm:linear-stability}.  For the upper
branch, apply the lower branch to $1-\alpha$, and reflect the resulting
slope $(1-\alpha)/p$ at level $n+1$.  Reflecting both descendants gives
\eqref{eq:four-descendants}.  The two conditions cover $(0,1)$ if
$A/D_n<1/2$.
head: environment

label: cor:binary-descendants
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Iterated descendants

title: Proof
body_md:
If $A/D_r<x<1-A/D_r$, both $x/p$ and $(p-1+x)/p$ lie in
$(A/D_{r+1},1-A/D_{r+1})$, since $D_{r+1}=pD_r$.
Thus both branches can be repeated indefinitely.  Their compositions
give \eqref{eq:binary-descendants}.  The numerators have an integer part
whose base-$p$ digits are $0$ or $p-1$.  Two such values can coincide
only if their integer parts and their fractional parts coincide; the
two possible fractional parts agree precisely when $\alpha=1/2$.
The count is not $4^t$: the two members of a reflection pair have the
same four descendants at the next step.
head: environment

label: cor:top-down
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Descent from the next level

title: Proof
body_md:
The lower band is the exact multiset identity
\eqref{eq:linear-slope-identity} for $r=n+1$; there is no room for
additional slopes in that band.  Reflecting at both levels gives the
upper band.  The count in each controlled band comes from
Corollary~\ref{thm:linear-stability}.  The consecutive contacts at $D_n,D_n+1$, considered at level
$n+1$, give a characteristic slope equal to $1/p$ in the $q$-normalization,
with exactly $D_n-1$ primitive slopes strictly below it.
Symmetry gives the same count at the other end.  Subtracting yields
$A$ in each excluded strip.
For \eqref{eq:top-down-higher}, use \eqref{eq:linear-slope-identity}
with $r=n+t$ and reflect at both levels.  There are
$p^tD_n-1$ primitive slopes at that level, proving the proportion.
head: environment

label: rem:progression-multiplicities
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:progression-multiplicities}
For other base curves it is natural to allow repeated arithmetic progressions
and their full multiplicities. A formulation sufficient for the applications
below is this: there are an integer $h\geq0$ and a level $n_0$ such that,
after adjoining $h$ zeros to $S_n$ to form $\widetilde S_n$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-progression}
 \widetilde S_n=\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{p^{n-n_0}-1}
 \frac{j+\widetilde S_{n_0}}{p^{n-n_0}}\qquad(n\geq n_0).
\end{equation}
Each occurrence of $\alpha\in\widetilde S_{n_0}$ generates the progression
$(\alpha+j)/p^{n-n_0}$, and the $h$ auxiliary zeros are removed afterward.
Definition~\ref{def:slope-stability} is the case $h=1$; its adjacent-level
grid slopes then occur once. In \eqref{eq:general-progression} they occur
$h$ times. Explicitly, for every sufficiently large $n$ the adjacent
identity is
\[
 S_{n+1}=\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{p-1}\frac{j+S_n}{p}
 \sqcup\bigsqcup_{\ell=1}^{h}
 \left\{\frac1p,\frac2p,\ldots,\frac{p-1}{p}\right\}.
\]
The $h$ zeros in the block $j=0$ have been removed; their translates
in the other $p-1$ blocks give the displayed grids. For our towers
with eventual minimal break ratios, $\#S_n=D_n-1$ and
$D_{n+1}=pD_n$. Counting both sides with multiplicities gives
\[pD_n-1=p(D_n-1)+h(p-1),\]
so necessarily $h=1$. Thus this formulation does not weaken
Definition~\ref{def:slope-stability} in the main setting of this paper.
Tails over $C_r$ will instead have $h=p^r$; see Remark~\ref{rem:intermediate-base}.
More general conventions may also allow a fixed exceptional multiset,
as in \cite[\S1.1]{KramerMillerUpton2023}. We do not require that additional
generality here. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, ``slope stable'' below
means Definition~\ref{def:slope-stability}.
head: environment
name: Arithmetic-progression slope stability

label: rem:intermediate-base
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:intermediate-base}
Fix $r\geq1$ and regard the tail as a $\mathbf Z_p$-tower over $C_r$.
Write $S_n^{(r)}$ for its primitive $q$-slope multiset at relative level $n$.
Artin induction and character independence give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-slopes}
 S_n^{(r)}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{p^r}S_{n+r}.
\end{equation}
Consequently the classical partial-stability statements pass to the tail
by shifting the level and multiplying multiplicities by $p^r$.
Full stability, when known for the original tower, passes in the
arithmetic-progression sense of Remark~\ref{rem:progression-multiplicities},
with $h=p^r$. Every $C_r$ has $p$-rank zero and is therefore nonordinary
when $g(C_r)>0$. In contrast, the relative upper breaks satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-breaks}
 s_n^{(r)}=p^rs_{n+r}-(2g(C_r)+p^r-1),
\end{equation}
so eventual minimal break ratios for the original tower imply
\[s_{n+1}^{(r)}-ps_n^{(r)}=(p-1)(2g(C_r)+p^r-1)>0\]
for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus tails of fully slope-stable polynomial
towers give progression-stable examples over nonordinary bases without
eventual minimal relative break ratios. These are inherited examples, not
results for arbitrary nonordinary bases; the classical induction argument
does not assert an analogous arbitrary-weight annular theorem over $C_r$.
We give the proof and a simple example next.
head: environment
name: Passage to an intermediate base curve

label: eq:tail-induction
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U_r$ be $C_r$ with the unique point above infinity removed. Then
$U_r\to\mathbf A^1$ is finite etale of degree $p^r$ and the Galois group of
the tail is $p^r\mathbf Z_p\simeq\mathbf Z_p$. A character $\psi$ of $p^r\mathbf Z_p$ of exact
order $p^n$ has precisely $p^r$ extensions $\chi$ to $\mathbf Z_p$, all of exact
order $p^{n+r}$: if $\psi(p^r)$ is a primitive $p^n$-th root of unity,
each of its $p^r$-th roots is primitive of order $p^{n+r}$.
The induced representation is the direct sum of these extensions.
Factoring the local Euler factors, or Artin induction, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-induction}
L_{U_r}(\psi,s)=\prod_{\chi|_{p^r\mathbf Z_p}=\psi}L_f(\chi,s).
\end{equation}
All factors on the right have the same slopes by
Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-basics}, proving \eqref{eq:tail-slopes}
with unchanged $q$-normalization. This proves the claimed transfer of
classical multiset identities. In particular the sharper left endpoint
for the tail is $1/p-A/D_{n+r+1}$ whenever the original comparison applies
at level $n+r$.

If the original tower is fully slope stable, repeating its block identity
$p^r$ times yields
\[
S_{n+1}^{(r)}=\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{p-1}\frac{j+S_n^{(r)}}p
\sqcup\bigsqcup_{\ell=1}^{p^r}\left\{\frac1p,\ldots,\frac{p-1}p\right\}.
\]
Adjoining $p^r$ zeros gives \eqref{eq:general-progression} by iteration.
Full stability here is inherited from a fully stable original tower;
the partial-stability theorem alone is not enough.

The Deuring--Shafarevich formula for the single totally ramified point gives
\[\operatorname{prank}(C_r)-1
=p^r\bigl(\operatorname{prank}(\mathbf P^1)-1\bigr)+(p^r-1)=-1.\]
Thus $\operatorname{prank}(C_r)=0$; compare \cite[Theorem 5.1]{Wan2019}.
For completeness, the conductor degree formula for a nontrivial
rank-one character on $C_r$ is $2g(C_r)-2$ plus its total Artin
conductor. There is one ramified point, rational over $\mathbf F_q$, and its
Artin conductor is the Swan conductor plus one, namely $s_n^{(r)}+1$.
Consequently
\[
 \deg L_{U_r}(\psi,s)=2g(C_r)-2+(s_n^{(r)}+1)
 =2g(C_r)-1+s_n^{(r)}.
\]
Each of the $p^r$ factors on the right of \eqref{eq:tail-induction}
has degree $s_{n+r}-1$. Taking degrees and solving for the relative
break gives
\[
 2g(C_r)-1+s_n^{(r)}=p^r(s_{n+r}-1),\qquad
 s_n^{(r)}=p^rs_{n+r}-(2g(C_r)+p^r-1),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:tail-breaks}. Subtracting $p$ times this identity
at level $n$ from its version at level $n+1$ gives
\[
 s_{n+1}^{(r)}-ps_n^{(r)}
 =p^r(s_{n+r+1}-ps_{n+r})+(p-1)(2g(C_r)+p^r-1).
\]
The first term vanishes for large $n$ under eventual minimal break
ratios, and the remaining term is positive because $r\geq1$.
This also explains why the necessity lemma
for Definition~\ref{def:slope-stability} cannot be applied after changing
the base and the grid multiplicity.

label: prop:old-block-radius
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: The first-block criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
At every level $r\geq n>m$, the contacts at $D_n,D_n+1$ give
exactly $D_n-1$ primitive slopes below $D_n/D_r=p^{n-r}$.
After the valuation change \eqref{eq:general-valuations}, equality
of these multisets is equivalent to equality of the first $D_n$
characteristic slopes.  The next common contact extends polygon
agreement through $D_n+1$.
Agreement of all higher polygons identifies that interval with
the limit.  Conversely, if every sufficiently large $N_n$ agrees
with the limit through $D_n+1$, then for $r\geq n$ both $N_n$ and
$N_r$ agree with it on that interval.  The same slope count gives
complete first-block propagation.
head: environment

label: prop:finite-block-stability
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Finite-block criterion for slope stability

title: Proof
body_md:
For (i), the common contact vertices at $bD_n$ and $bD_n+1$ give
exactly $bD_n-1$ primitive slopes of level $n+1$ below $b/p$.
Indeed, the slope of their joining segment, after division by
$a(p-1)p^n$, is $b/p$.  The preceding slopes are strictly smaller
and the following slopes strictly larger, by the Hodge lower bound;
the contact theorem is recalled in Proposition~\ref{prop:general-Hodge-contact}.
The first $bD_n$ characteristic slopes of $N_n$ consist of zero,
the $b$ translates of $S_n$, and $b-1$ grid slopes, in the
normalization of Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence}.  Dividing
by $a(p-1)p^n$ proves (i).

For (ii), the first $p$ level-$n$ characteristic blocks have total length
$pD_n=D_{n+1}$.  After each interval of this length, the slope
sequence of either polygon repeats with the same additive shift
$a(p-1)p^n$: for $N_n$ this is $p$ repetitions of its period of length $D_n$,
and for $N_{n+1}$ it is one repetition.  Equality on that common
period therefore implies equality on the whole half-line.
Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence} gives the assertion.

For (iii), divide the first $pD_n$ slopes of both polygons by
$a(p-1)p^n$ and remove the initial zero.  Each resulting multiset
has $pD_n-1$ elements and is invariant under $\alpha\mapsto1-\alpha$.
For $N_{n+1}$ this is the functional equation.  For $N_n$ it follows
from $S_n=1-S_n$, since reflection exchanges the blocks $j$ and
$p-1-j$ and pairs the grid slopes.  A symmetric ordered multiset
is determined by its lower half and its cardinality.  Agreement on
the first $\lceil p/2\rceil D_n$ characteristic slopes includes that
lower half and the initial zero.  Reflection determines the remainder,
reducing the assertion to (ii).
head: environment

label: lem:head-stability
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:head-stability}
Assume $p>2$.  If $n\geq2$, $n>m$, and
$(p-2)p^{n-1}>C/\delta$, then the
$\pi_{\chi_r}$-adic polygon of $C_{f^{<n}}^*(\chi_r,s)$ is independent
of $r\geq n$.  It equals $N_n$.
head: environment
name: Stability of the finite truncation

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from \cite[Proposition 8.3]{KostersZhu2018}, with highest
Witt level at most $n-1$.  We recall the comparison behind that result.
Use the parameters of Definition~\ref{def:AH-parameters}.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:pi-congruence}, they satisfy
\[
 \pi_i(T)=\pi_0(T)^{p^i}+pT\,g_i(T),\qquad g_i(T)\in\mathbf Z_p[[T]].
\]

In a Dwork determinant term write $w$ for the sum of the parameter
weights, assigning formal weight $p^i$ to $\pi_i(T)$. A term contributing to
the coefficient of $s^k$ has $w\geq h(k)$. After evaluation at
$T=\pi_{\chi_r}$, replacing one parameter $\pi_i(\pi_{\chi_r})$
by its error raises the valuation above this weight by at least the
following amount. Here $0\leq i<n$, because we are working with the
finite truncation $f^{<n}$:
\[
 (p-1)p^{r-1}+1-p^i
 \geq (p-2)p^{n-1}+1>C/\delta.
\]
All such errors therefore lie above $h(k)+C/\delta$.

After these replacements, the coefficient is a power series in
$\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_r})$ whose integral coefficients are independent of
$r$.  Below the height $h(k)+C/\delta$, its valuation is determined by the
first coefficient that is a unit modulo $p$.  A coefficient divisible
by $p$ cannot interfere, since $v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(p)>C/\delta$.
Thus every coefficient point that can be a polygon vertex has a
valuation independent of $r$.  The common upper bound
\eqref{eq:general-contact} then gives equality of polygons.
At $r=n$ the truncation and the original tower agree, giving $N_n$.
head: environment

label: lem:tail-estimate
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Tail estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
At a character of order $p^r$, only levels $i<r$ are active and the
parameter at level $i$ has $v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}$-valuation $p^i$.
Use the closed-minor expansion and its valuation calculation in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-minor-bound}, with $g(x)=x/\delta$.
Each determinant term uses $a$ sets of $k$ distinct nonnegative indices. The total monomial degree
is $p-1$ times the sum of these indices, because the row and column
index sets are cyclically matched. Coefficient Frobenius preserves
all valuations.

In the difference of the two coefficients, every surviving term
contains a monomial of degree $\ell$ from some level $i\geq n$.
Mark one occurrence and let $u$ be its matrix row. The index set
containing $u$ has sum at least
\[
 u+\frac{(k-1)(k-2)}2=\frac{k(k-1)}2+u-k+1;
\]
each of the other $a-1$ sets has sum at least $k(k-1)/2$.
The base degree estimate is
Corollary~\ref{cor:classical-reduced-coefficients}. For the marked
occurrence, use its actual parameter
valuation $p^i$ instead of $\ell/\delta$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-index-inequality}
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(\text{term})
 \geq h(k)+\frac{(p-1)(u-k+1)}{\delta}+p^i-\frac{\ell}{\delta}.
\end{equation}
Since $i\geq n>m$, the integer $\delta p^i$ is divisible by $p$
and is at least $pD_n$. Moreover, an occurrence of this monomial
in row $u$ and column $j\geq0$ has $\ell\leq pu-j\leq pu$.
Since $pu$ is divisible by $p$ while the reduced exponent $\ell$
is not, equality with $pu$ is impossible. Together with
$\ell\leq\delta p^i$, this gives
\[
 \delta p^i-\ell\geq1,\qquad \ell\leq pu-1.
\]
If $u\geq D_n$, \eqref{eq:tail-index-inequality} immediately gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(\text{term})
 \geq h(k)+\frac{(p-1)(D_n-k+1)}{\delta}+\frac1\delta.
\]
If $u<D_n$, use $i\geq n$ and $p^n=pD_n/\delta$ to obtain
\[
 p^i-\frac\ell\delta
 \geq\frac{pD_n}{\delta}-\frac{pu-1}{\delta}
 =\frac{p(D_n-u)+1}{\delta}.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{eq:tail-index-inequality} gives the stronger bound
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(\text{term})
 \geq h(k)+\frac{(p-1)(D_n-k+1)}{\delta}
             +\frac{D_n-u+1}{\delta}.
\]
Both cases prove the strict estimate, and hence the weaker one.
The convergent Fredholm sum preserves these lower bounds.
If there is no surviving term, the difference is zero.
head: environment

label: cor:degree-eleven-loss
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:degree-eleven-loss}
Suppose $p=q=7$ and $\delta=11$. For every tower in the setup of
Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}, and every $n\geq2$,
\[
 N_r\big|_{[0,D_n-10]}=N_n\big|_{[0,D_n-10]}
 \quad(r\geq n),\qquad R_n\geq D_n-10,
 \qquad D_n=11\cdot7^{n-1}.
\]
The loss ten is optimal, as the example in
Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss} will show.
head: environment
name: A sharper loss in degree eleven

title: Proof
body_md:
Here the maximal normalized degree is attained at level zero: at a
positive level $i$, attaining degree $11\cdot7^i$ would violate the
reduced condition on the exponents. Thus $m=0$, $d=11$, and
$C/\delta=75/11$. Since $5\cdot7^{n-1}>75/11$ for $n\geq2$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:head-stability} identifies the polygon of $f^{<n}$
at every conductor $7^r$, $r\geq n$, with $N_n$.

For $1\leq k\leq D_n-12$, the weaker tail bound
\eqref{eq:tail-estimate} already gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}\bigl(b_k(f,\pi_{\chi_r})-b_k(f^{<n},\pi_{\chi_r})\bigr)
 \geq h(k)+\frac{78}{11}
 >h(k)+\frac{75}{11}\geq N_n(k).
\]
The two remaining indices $D_n-11$ and $D_n-10$ are congruent to
zero and one modulo eleven. They are common Hodge contacts, so
$N_n(k)=h(k)$ there, whereas the tail bound is still strictly
larger than $h(k)$. Every coefficient perturbation through
$M=D_n-10$ therefore lies strictly above $N_n$.
Consequently the vertices of $N_n$ through $M$ are preserved and
no coefficient point in this interval drops below it.
The common contact at $M$ is a vertex, so later coefficient points
cannot change this initial part of the lower convex hull.
This proves the displayed equality for every $r\geq n$.
Passing to the local limit gives $R_n\geq D_n-10$.
head: environment

label: thm:all-slope-propagation
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Propagation of the whole primitive multiset

title: Proof
body_md:
The bound $N_\infty(j)-h(j)\leq C/\delta$ follows from
\eqref{eq:general-contact}. Since $(p-1)A\geq C$, the criterion is
automatic for $j\geq A$. When $A=0$ there are no indices to check.
Choose $n>m$ so large that
\[
 D_n>A,\qquad D_n\geq2A,\qquad n\geq2,\qquad
 (p-2)p^{n-1}>C/\delta.
\]
The condition $p>2$ ensures that such levels exist. The classical
agreement theorem gives $N_n=N_\infty$ through $D_n-A\geq A$;
thus all the required indices $j<A$ agree with the limit. For
$j\geq A$ the common upper bound $C/\delta$ again suffices. Hence
\[
 N_n(j)-h(j)\leq\frac{(p-1)j}{\delta}\qquad(j\geq1).
\]

We now use reflection within the first primitive block.  For
$1\leq k\leq D_n$, slope symmetry and the initial zero slope imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reflected-excess}
 N_n(k)-h(k)
 =N_n(D_n-k+1)-h(D_n-k+1).
\end{equation}
To verify the shift by one, list the $D_n-1$ primitive slopes in
increasing order as $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{D_n-1}$. The functional
equation says $\alpha_i+\alpha_{D_n-i}=1$. Therefore the sum of all
primitive slopes is $(D_n-1)/2$, and, for $j=k-1$, the sum of the
largest $j$ is
\[
 \sum_{i=D_n-j}^{D_n-1}\alpha_i
 =j-\sum_{i=1}^{j}\alpha_i.
\]
The characteristic polygon has an initial zero slope. Its ordinate
at $k$ is consequently $a(p-1)p^{n-1}$ times the sum of the smallest
$k-1$ primitive slopes. Its ordinate at $D_n-k+1$ uses all primitive
slopes except the largest $k-1$. Subtracting cancels the common
smallest-slope sum and yields
\[
 \begin{split}
 N_n(D_n-k+1)-N_n(k)
 &=\frac{a(p-1)D_n}{\delta}
       \left(\frac{D_n-1}{2}-(k-1)\right)\\
 &=\frac{a(p-1)D_n}{2\delta}(D_n-2k+1).
 \end{split}
\]
Direct substitution in $h(x)=a(p-1)x(x-1)/(2\delta)$ gives the same
difference for $h(D_n-k+1)-h(k)$, proving
\eqref{eq:reflected-excess}. Apply the preceding upper bound for
$N_n(j)-h(j)$ at $j=D_n-k+1$ and then use this identity. We obtain
\[
 N_n(k)\leq h(k)+\frac{(p-1)(D_n-k+1)}{\delta}
 \qquad(1\leq k\leq D_n).
\]
This estimate becomes stronger near the right endpoint, exactly
where the direct upper bound by $(p-1)k/\delta$ would be too weak.
The strict tail bound \eqref{eq:strict-tail-estimate} puts every
coefficient difference between $f$ and $f^{<n}$ strictly above this
polygon through $D_n$.  The finite truncation has polygon $N_n$ at
all higher conductors, by Lemma~\ref{lem:head-stability}.  Preserving
its vertices, with the common endpoint at $D_n$, proves the first
identity in \eqref{eq:all-slope-propagation}.  Taking the local limit identifies this restriction
with $N_\infty$.  The contact at $D_n+1$ extends the agreement
and gives the exact slope identity, as in the proof of
Corollary~\ref{thm:linear-stability}.
head: environment

label: cor:small-degree
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:small-degree}
Over $\mathbf F_p$ with $p>2$, suppose
\[
 1\leq\deg f_0=d\leq6,\qquad \deg f_i\leq dp^i\quad(i\geq1).
\]
Then \eqref{eq:full-propagation-criterion} holds, so
\eqref{eq:all-slope-propagation} holds for all sufficiently large $n$.
No positive degree gap on the tail is required.
head: environment
name: Small initial degree over the prime field

title: Proof
body_md:
Here $a=1$ and $m=0$.  For $j=td+u$, $1\leq u\leq d$, the chord
bound \eqref{eq:general-chord-gap} gives
\[
 N_\infty(j)-h(j)\leq\frac{p-1}{2\delta}(u-1)(d-u).
\]
For $u=1$ or $u=d$ this is zero: these are contact indices.
At an interior integer $2\leq u\leq d-1$, use $d\leq6$ to write
\[
 (u-1)(d-u)-2u
 \leq (u-1)(6-u)-2u
 =-(u-2)(u-3)\leq0.
\]
The last inequality uses integrality: for $u=2,3$ the product is
zero, and for every integer $u\geq4$ it is positive.
Thus $(u-1)(d-u)\leq2u$, and the chord bound becomes
\[
 N_\infty(j)-h(j)\leq\frac{(p-1)u}{\delta}
 \leq\frac{(p-1)j}{\delta},
\]
since $j=td+u\geq u$. Contacts and interior indices together exhaust
all positive integers, proving the criterion.
head: environment

label: prop:degree-eight-coefficient
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:degree-eight-coefficient}
Over $\mathbf F_7$, suppose
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f_0(X)=X^8+a_6X^6+a_5X^5+\cdots+a_1X,\qquad a_6\ne0,\\
 \deg f_i\leq8\cdot7^i\quad(i\geq1).
 \end{gathered}
\]
Then \eqref{eq:full-propagation-criterion} holds, independently of
the higher Witt coefficients.  Consequently every primitive slope
eventually propagates by division by seven, with its multiplicity.
head: environment
name: A coefficient condition in characteristic seven

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider only the Teichm\"uller polynomial $f_0$.
At a character of order seven put $\pi=\zeta_7-1$.  The coefficient
of $s$ in its primitive $L$-function is the first exponential sum,
and
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathbf F_7}\zeta_7^{f_0(x)}
 \equiv-[a_6]\pi\pmod{\pi^2}.
\]
Indeed the constant term seven vanishes modulo $\pi^2$, and
$\sum_x f_0(x)=-a_6$ in $\mathbf F_7$.  Thus the smallest primitive
$7$-adic slope is at most $1/6$, and symmetry makes the largest at
least $5/6$.

Let $P$ be the $\pi$-adic characteristic polygon of this polynomial
tower.  It is independent of the character conductor from the first
level: the Davis--Wan--Xiao bound is
$(8-1)^2/(8\cdot8)=49/64<1$
\cite[Theorems 1.2 and 3.8]{DavisWanXiao2016}.
We may therefore compute $P$ at conductor seven, where
$v_\pi(7)=6$. Its first eight slopes are zero and six times the
seven primitive slopes. Their total is $6\cdot7/2=21$.
The smallest primitive slope is at most $1/6$, and the largest is
at least $5/6$, so
\[
 P(1)=0,\qquad P(2)\leq6\cdot\frac16=1,\qquad
 P(7)\leq21-6\cdot\frac56=16,\qquad P(8)=21.
\]
The chord from $(2,1)$ to $(7,16)$ has slope three. Convexity places
$P$ below this chord, giving $P(j)\leq3j-5$ for $2\leq j\leq7$.
In this case $h(j)=3j(j-1)/8$ and $(p-1)/\delta=3/4$.  Direct subtraction
shows, for $2\leq j\leq7$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 h(j)+\tfrac34j-(3j-5)&=(3j^2-21j+40)/8>0,\\
 h(j)+\tfrac34(9-j)-(3j-5)&=(3j^2-33j+94)/8>0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For an explicit positive margin, these two expressions equal
\[
 \frac38\left(j-\frac72\right)^2+\frac{13}{32},\qquad
 \frac38\left(j-\frac{11}{2}\right)^2+\frac{13}{32},
\]
respectively. At $j=1,8$ we have $P(j)=h(j)$, and both added terms
$3j/4$ and $3(9-j)/4$ are positive. Thus $P$ lies strictly below
both comparison bounds at every integer $1\leq j\leq8$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tail-estimate} to the full tower and its
truncation $f^{<1}=f_0$; this is allowed because $m=0$. For every
character conductor, the coefficient differences through index eight
have valuation at least
\[
 h(j)+\frac34(9-j)+\frac18>P(j),\qquad1\leq j\leq8.
\]
At each vertex of $P$ the original coefficient therefore retains
its valuation, while no other coefficient can move below $P$.
The common contact at eight prevents later coefficients from
altering this initial convex hull. Hence the full tower has polygon
$P$ on $[0,8]$ at every conductor, and passage to the local limit
gives $N_\infty=P$ there. The first comparison bound proves
\eqref{eq:full-propagation-criterion} on this interval. Finally
$A=8\lceil49/64\rceil=8$, so the criterion requires only
$1\leq j<8$, all of which have now been checked.
head: environment

label: def:spectral-curve
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:spectral-curve}
Let $\mathscr W=\{T\in\mathbf C_p:|T|_p<1\}$ be the rigid analytic
weight disc.  The spectral curve of the tower is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-curve}
 \mathscr X_f=
 \{(T,s)\in\mathscr W\times\{|s|_p<q\}:C_f^*(T,s)=0\},
\end{equation}
with the analytic structure defined by this equation.  Its weight map
is the projection $(T,s)\mapsto T$.
Its analyticity on this domain is proved in
Proposition~\ref{prop:analytic-domain}.
Since $C_f^*(T,0)=1$, every point of the curve has $s\ne0$,
and $s^{-1}$ is its reciprocal-root coordinate.
head: environment
name: Spectral curve and weight map

label: def:finite-flat-part
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:finite-flat-part}
Let $V$ be a weight annulus.  A spectral part of degree $r$ over
$V$ is an open and closed analytic subspace of the spectral curve
restricted to weights in $V$, whose projection to $V$ is finite and flat
of degree $r$.  Equivalently, on suitable affinoid neighborhoods
$U\subset V$, its coordinate algebra is a finite locally free
$\mathcal O(U)$-module of rank $r$.
Fiber lengths, and hence slope multiplicities, are counted with
their scheme-theoretic multiplicities.
head: environment
name: Finite flat spectral part

label: lem:relative-slope-factor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:relative-slope-factor}
Let $U$ be a closed affinoid annulus over $\mathbf C_p$ contained in
$0<|T|_p<1$, and give its reduced affinoid algebra
$B=\mathcal O(U)$ the complete supremum norm.  Let $\rho<a$ be
rational.  Suppose that there is $\eta>0$ such that, in every
analytic fiber over $U$, the first $r$ reciprocal-root
$v_p$-slopes are at most $\rho-\eta$, and every subsequent slope
is at least $\rho+\eta$.
Then the zeros with $v_p(s^{-1})<\rho$ form a finite flat part of
degree $r$ over $U$.  Its algebra is free over $B$ with a basis
of $r$ elements.
head: environment
name: A gap gives a polynomial factor

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $b\in\mathbf C_p$ with $v_p(b)=-\rho$, and put $s=bZ$.
Since $\rho<a$, Proposition~\ref{prop:analytic-domain} gives
\[
 C_f^*(T,bZ)=\sum_{j\geq0}a_j(T)Z^j\in B\langle Z\rangle.
\]
The coefficient norms tend to zero uniformly on $U$, by analyticity
on the product of this closed weight annulus and the closed disc
$|s|_p\leq p^\rho<q$. Scaling $s=bZ$ subtracts $\rho j$ from the
valuation of the coefficient of degree $j$. The slope gap makes $r$
a vertex in every fiber, and it makes the scaled coefficient at $r$
strictly smaller in valuation than every other coefficient.  The supporting line of slope $\rho$
therefore gives, for $j\ne r$ and every analytic point $T_0$ of the
affinoid spectrum,
\[
 |a_j(T_0)/a_r(T_0)|_p\leq p^{-\eta|j-r|}\leq p^{-\eta}<1.
\]
In particular $a_r(T)$ is nowhere zero, hence invertible in $B$.
Because $B$ is reduced, its supremum norm gives the same uniform
bound for these coefficient ratios.  Consequently
\[
 G(T,Z):=a_r(T)^{-1}C_f^*(T,bZ),
 \qquad \|G(T,Z)-Z^r\|\leq p^{-\eta}<1.
\]

Here is the precise preparation argument needed in this setting.
Over the complete nonarchimedean Banach algebra $B$, the
inequality $\|G(T,Z)-Z^r\|<1$ gives division by $G(T,Z)$
with a unique remainder of degree less than $r$.
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Consider the map
\[
  (Q(T,Z),R(T,Z))\longmapsto Q(T,Z)Z^r+R(T,Z),
\]
where
\[
 Q(T,Z)\in B\langle Z\rangle,\quad
 R(T,Z)\in B[Z],\quad\deg_Z R(T,Z)<r.
\]
It is an isometric isomorphism for the maximum norm.  Replacing
$Z^r$ by $G(T,Z)$ perturbs this map by $(Q(T,Z),R(T,Z))\mapsto Q(T,Z)(G(T,Z)-Z^r)$, of
operator norm less than one.  Its inverse exists by the
convergent geometric series for that operator.  Dividing $Z^r$
itself gives
\[
 Z^r=Q(T,Z)G(T,Z)+R(T,Z),\qquad \|Q(T,Z)-1\|<1,\quad\|R(T,Z)\|<1.
\]
Thus $Q(T,Z)$ is a unit, and $P(T,Z)=Z^r-R(T,Z)$ is a monic polynomial of
degree $r$, with all its lower coefficients of norm less than
one.  This proves the relative Weierstrass factorization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-Weierstrass}
 C_f^*(T,bZ)=U_0(T,Z)P(T,Z),\qquad
 P(T,Z)=Z^r+c_{r-1}(T)Z^{r-1}+\cdots+c_0(T),
\end{equation}
where $U_0(T,Z)=a_r(T)Q(T,Z)^{-1}$ is an analytic unit.
All roots of $P(T,Z)$ lie strictly inside the unit $Z$-disc.
The same division argument for $P(T,Z)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-free-algebra}
 B\langle Z\rangle/(P(T,Z))
 \simeq B[Z]/(P(T,Z))
 \simeq B\oplus BZ\oplus\cdots\oplus BZ^{r-1}
 \quad\text{as $B$-modules}.
\end{equation}
The middle algebra is free because division by a monic polynomial
works over any coefficient ring: every class has a representative
of degree less than $r$, and such a representative is unique.
Thus the projection is finite, with free algebra of rank $r$.
Tensoring with this algebra is, as a module operation, taking
$r$ copies of the original module; it preserves exact sequences.
This is precisely the flatness condition.
The argument uses monicity and remains valid at repeated roots;
separability is not required.  A count of roots alone would not
supply this proof of flatness.

The zeros of $P(T,Z)$ are exactly the zeros of $C_f^*(T,bZ)$ with
$|s|_p<p^\rho$, or equivalently $v_p(s^{-1})<\rho$.
There are no zeros on the separating circle.  Hence this subset
and its complement give an admissible open and closed
decomposition of the zero locus over $U$.
head: environment

label: def:spectral-cutoff
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:spectral-cutoff}
Let $K\geq1$ be a vertex abscissa of $N_\infty$, and let
$\lambda_K=N_\infty(K)-N_\infty(K-1)$ be its $K$-th slope,
counted with multiplicity.  Over the annulus $\mathscr W_K$, define
\[
 \mathscr X_{\leq K}
 =\{(T,s)\in\mathscr X_f:T\in\mathscr W_K,\
           v_p(s^{-1})\leq\lambda_Kv_p(T)\},
\]
with the induced analytic structure.  The theorem below shows that
this locus is open and closed and consists of the first $K$ zeros
in every fiber, ordered by reciprocal-root valuation.  Thus $K$
is an index cutoff, not a numerical slope bound.  The vertex
condition ensures that the cutoff does not divide a repeated slope.
head: environment
name: The first \texorpdfstring{$K$}{K} spectral slopes

label: thm:spectral-pieces
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:spectral-pieces}
Let $K\geq1$ be a vertex abscissa of $N_\infty$, and list its
first $K$ slopes with multiplicity as $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K$.
Here $K$ counts slopes; it is not a slope value.
The projection of the locus in Definition~\ref{def:spectral-cutoff},
\[
 \mathscr X_{\leq K}\longrightarrow\mathscr W_K
\]
is finite flat of degree $K$, and this locus is open and closed
in the spectral curve over $\mathscr W_K$.
It is the disjoint union of finite flat parts indexed by the
distinct slopes $\lambda$ among these $K$ slopes, characterized by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-slope-law}
 v_p(s^{-1})=\lambda v_p(T).
\end{equation}
The degree of the part for $\lambda$ is its full multiplicity,
which is at most $\max\{1,d-1\}$.
These decompositions agree under restriction when $K$ increases
through vertices and the annulus shrinks.
If $K=M\geq2$ is a contact index, the same assertions hold on the
larger annulus \eqref{eq:annular-contact-width}.
head: environment
name: Finite flat spectral pieces

title: Proof
body_md:
Write the slopes of $N_\infty$ as
$\lambda_1\leq\lambda_2\leq\cdots$, counted with multiplicity.
Since $K$ is a vertex, $\lambda_K<\lambda_{K+1}$.
Corollary~\ref{cor:annulus-width} gives agreement through $K+1$,
and therefore at every $T\in\mathscr W_K$ the first $K+1$
specialized slopes are
\[
 v_p(T)\lambda_1,\ldots,v_p(T)\lambda_{K+1}.
\]
All are strictly less than $a$.

Fix a weight $T_0$ in this annulus.  Choose positive rational
$u<v$ sufficiently close to $v_p(T_0)$, and a rational $\rho$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-slope-cut}
 \lambda_K v<\rho<\lambda_{K+1}u,
 \qquad 0<u\leq v<\varepsilon_K,
 \qquad \rho<a.
\end{equation}
This is possible because $\lambda_Kv_p(T_0)<
\lambda_{K+1}v_p(T_0)<a$; choose $\rho$ between the first two
values and then shrink the interval $[u,v]$ around $v_p(T_0)$.
On the closed weight annulus $u\leq v_p(T)\leq v$, the first $K$
slopes are below $\rho$ and all subsequent slopes are above it.
The positive distances from $\rho$ to the two bounds have a
positive minimum, which supplies the $\eta$ in
Lemma~\ref{lem:relative-slope-factor}. It gives a finite free piece of
degree $K$ there.  Such sufficiently thin closed annuli form an
admissible cover of $\mathscr W_K$.

On an overlap, express both polynomial factors in the original
coordinate $s$ and normalize their constant coefficients to one.
This is possible because $s=0$ is never a zero.  In each fiber
they are the same polynomial: their roots, with multiplicities,
are exactly the first $K$ zeros.  Their analytic coefficients
therefore agree on the overlap, since its affinoid algebra is
reduced.  The factors and the quotient algebras they define glue,
so the resulting identification preserves the analytic structure,
including any nonreduced structure at repeated roots.  Finiteness
and flatness are local on the base, so the glued projection
$\mathscr X_{\leq K}\longrightarrow\mathscr W_K$ is finite flat
of degree $K$.

To obtain the individual slope parts, perform the same construction
at every strict gap among $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K$.
The successive polynomial factors isolate each distinct value
$\lambda$, with its entire multiplicity $r_\lambda$.
Locally their algebras again have the form
$B[Z]/(P_\lambda)$ with $P_\lambda$ monic of degree $r_\lambda$.
They are therefore free of rank $r_\lambda$, proving finite flatness
of every part, not just of their union.
Their characterization is precisely
\[
 v_p(s^{-1})=\lambda v_p(T).
\]
Every contact of $N_\infty$ is a strict vertex, so an edge lies
between consecutive contacts.  Their spacings are one and $d-1$
when $d>1$, and one when $d=1$.  It follows that
$r_\lambda\leq\max\{1,d-1\}$.

Finally, if $K'<K$ is another vertex, restriction to
$\mathscr W_K\subseteq\mathscr W_{K'}$ selects the same first $K'$
zeros in either construction.  Uniqueness proves compatibility
of the decompositions as the annulus shrinks.

For the larger annulus at a contact $M$, the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:annular-agreement} gives a strict gap even without
determining the next slope.  The first $M$ specialized
slopes have maximum at most $\frac{a(p-1)v_p(T)}{\delta}(M-1)$, whereas the next
slope is at least $a\min\{\frac{(p-1)v_p(T)M}{\delta},1\}$.
The first bound is strictly smaller than the second and than $a$.
Around each weight these continuous bounds allow a uniform cut
$\rho<a$ exactly as above.  The same polynomial factorization,
free-algebra argument, and gluing therefore prove the contact
version of the theorem.
head: environment

label: rem:geometric-scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:geometric-scope}
The finite flat parts can be ramified or nonreduced, and a part
need not be connected or irreducible.  A repeated slope cannot be
split canonically by valuation into smaller degrees.  No assertion
of etaleness is made.
The annulus depends on $K$; the theorem does not give one annulus
on which all infinitely many limiting slopes occur inside $|s|_p<q$.
It also makes no assertion about the remaining zeros near that
boundary.  In the polynomial case, Davis--Wan--Xiao obtain a
decomposition on a fixed boundary annulus using global slope
stability and an entire characteristic family
\cite[Theorem 4.2]{DavisWanXiao2016}.  The present result controls
each finite initial portion under eventual minimal breaks alone.
head: environment
name: What the decomposition asserts

label: prop:classical-fiber
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: The spectral fiber at a classical point

title: Proof
body_md:
The first factor in \eqref{eq:general-C} has slopes zero and
$S_n\subset(0,1)$ in the $q$-valuation, and degree $D_n$.
Every root contributed by a later $q$-translate has reciprocal
$q$-valuation at least one and is outside $|s|_p<q$.
The later factors form an analytic unit on that open disc.
This proves the fiber description.
The normalization follows from
$v_p(T_0)=1/((p-1)p^{n-1})$ and $v_q=v_p/a$.
head: environment

label: cor:conductor-spectral-pieces
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:conductor-spectral-pieces}
Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{thm:linear-stability}, the first
$D_n-A$ zeros form a finite flat spectral part over the whole annulus
\eqref{eq:classical-annulus}, decomposed according to the limiting slopes.
head: environment
name: Finite flat pieces over the conductor annuli

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $K=D_n-A$. For $K\geq2$, inequality
\eqref{eq:annular-classical-inequality} is precisely the strict contact
bound needed in Theorem~\ref{thm:spectral-pieces} at $K$. In particular, even at
the included inner boundary of the conductor annulus, the slope
separation remains strict; this is why that boundary may be included.
If $K=1$, the polygon in \eqref{eq:uniform-gauss} has a strict vertex
at one, and $b_1(T_0)$ is a unit. Thus the zero slope is separated from
the next slope at every weight in the annulus. Lemma~\ref{lem:relative-slope-factor}
and the same gluing argument give a finite flat part of degree one.
head: environment

label: prop:width-leading
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:width-leading}
The width in Corollary~\ref{cor:annulus-width} satisfies
\[
 \varepsilon_K\sim\frac{\delta}{(p-1)K}.
\]
For annuli on which the first $K$ normalized slopes equal those
of $N_\infty$ and all their zeros remain in $|s|_p<q$, the leading
constant $\delta/(p-1)$ cannot be increased.
This statement does not assert optimality of the additive constant
in the denominator of \eqref{eq:annulus-width}.
head: environment
name: The natural geometric scale

title: Proof
body_md:
The difference $N_\infty(k)-h(k)$ is bounded between zero and
$C/\delta$.  Subtracting the heights at $K$ and $K-1$ therefore gives
\[
 \lambda_K=N_\infty(K)-N_\infty(K-1)
 =\frac{a(p-1)}{\delta}K+O(1).
\]
If widths $c/K+o(K^{-1})$ were possible with $c>\delta/(p-1)$,
choose $c'$ with $\delta/(p-1)<c'<c$ and weights of valuation
$v_p(T)=c'/K$ (or arbitrarily close rational valuations).
For large $K$ these belong to the asserted annulus, but the
$K$-th reciprocal root would have valuation
$v_p(T)\lambda_K\longrightarrow \frac{a(p-1)c'}{\delta}>a$.
Its zero would lie outside $|s|_p<q$, a contradiction.
The claimed asymptotic for our width follows directly from
\eqref{eq:annulus-width}.
head: environment

label: prop:breaks
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:breaks}
The Witt vector \eqref{eq:main-witt-vector} is reduced.  The associated tower
is unramified over $\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf F_p}$, totally ramified at infinity, and has upper
breaks
\[
 s_n=(p+1)p^{n-1}.
\]
For a character $\chi_n$ of order $p^n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L-degree}
 \deg L(\chi_n,s)=(p+1)p^{n-1}-1.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every exponent in \eqref{eq:main-witt-vector} is prime to $p$:
$p+1\equiv1\pmod p$ and $(p+1)p^j-2\equiv-2\pmod p$ for $j\geq1$.
Thus the presentation is reduced.  The normalized degrees are
\[
 p+1
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{(p+1)p^j-2}{p^j}
 =p+1-\frac{2}{p^j}<p+1.
\]
Hence the unique dominant normalized degree is $p+1$, attained by the unit
coefficient of $[X]^{p+1}$.  Formula~\eqref{eq:conductor-formula} gives the
upper break $(p+1)p^{n-1}$, and the degree formula for primitive $L$-functions gives
\eqref{eq:L-degree}.
head: environment

label: cor:genus
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:genus}
The genus of the $n$-th layer is
\[
 g_n=\frac{p^{2n}-p^n}{2}.
\]
In particular, the tower has minimal break ratios and is genus stable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The primitive part at exact conductor $p^r$ occurs with multiplicity
$\varphi(p^r)=(p-1)p^{r-1}$.  Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 2g_n
 &=\sum_{r=1}^n\varphi(p^r)
     \bigl((p+1)p^{r-1}-1\bigr)\\
 &=(p^2-1)\sum_{r=1}^n p^{2r-2}
   -(p-1)\sum_{r=1}^n p^{r-1}\\
 &=p^{2n}-p^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
head: environment

label: prop:Hodge-contact
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Kosters--Zhu Hodge and contact bounds

label: prop:low-order-splitting
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:low-order-splitting}
Below weighted order $4/(p+1)$, the specialized splitting function
is represented by the residue series \eqref{eq:En-definition}.
More precisely, the sum of contributions with $X$-degree $\ell$ and
$b=0$ or $1$ tail occurrences has, after division by
$\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})^{(\ell+2b)/(p+1)}$, the leading
residue $[z^bX^\ell]\mathcal E_n$.
Whenever such contributions occur, $(\ell+2b)/(p+1)$ is an
integer. All omitted terms have weighted order at least $4/(p+1)$.
head: environment
name: The first two weighted orders

title: Proof
body_md:
Write
\[
 E(U)=\sum_{r\geq0}a_rU^r,\qquad
 a_r\in\mathbf Z_p,\qquad a_0=a_1=1,
\]
and let $e_r$ be the reduction of $a_r$ modulo $p$.
We examine the product
\[
 E\!\left(\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})X^{p+1}\right)
 \prod_{j=1}^{n-1}
 E\!\left(\pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})X^{(p+1)p^j-2}\right).
\]

First, we determine which terms can have weighted order less than
$4/(p+1)$. A term from the dominant factor is
$a_r\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})^rX^{(p+1)r}$.
Since $v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n}))=1$, its weighted order is
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(a_r)+r-\frac{(p+1)r}{p+1}
 =v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(a_r)\geq0.
\]
Similarly, the term obtained by taking the $r$-th power in the
level-$j$ tail factor has weighted order
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(a_r)+rp^j
 -\frac{r((p+1)p^j-2)}{p+1}\geq\frac{2r}{p+1}.
\]
Weighted orders add under multiplication. Thus any product using at
least two tail occurrences has weighted order at least $4/(p+1)$.
This includes both a quadratic term from one tail factor and linear
terms from two different tail factors. Consequently, below the stated
cutoff, only the following expression matters:
\[
 E\!\left(\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})X^{p+1}\right)
 \left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
 \pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})X^{(p+1)p^j-2}\right).
\]

Next, we justify replacing each tail parameter by a power of
$\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})$. By \eqref{eq:pi-error},
\[
 \pi_j(T)-\pi_0(T)^{p^j}\in pT\mathbf Z_p[[T]].
\]
Since $v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(p)=(p-1)p^{n-1}$ and
$v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(\pi_{\chi_n})=1$, this gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}\!\left(
 \pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})-\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})^{p^j}\right)
 \geq(p-1)p^{n-1}+1.
\]
After attaching the corresponding power of $X$, the error has
weighted order at least
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &(p-1)p^{n-1}+1-\frac{(p+1)p^j-2}{p+1}\\
 &\qquad\geq(p-2)p^{n-1}+1+\frac2{p+1}>\frac4{p+1},
 \end{aligned}
\]
because $j<n$. Multiplication by terms from the dominant factor
cannot lower this order, since those terms have nonnegative
weighted order.

It remains to identify the residues. With no tail occurrence, a term
of degree $\ell=(p+1)r$ has coefficient
$a_r\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})^r$.
With one occurrence from level $j$, its degree and coefficient,
after the justified replacement, are
\[
 \ell=(p+1)(r+p^j)-2,\qquad
 a_r\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})^{r+p^j}.
\]
Thus in either case, with $b=0$ or $1$, the power extracted from
the coefficient is
\[
 \pi_0(\pi_{\chi_n})^{(\ell+2b)/(p+1)}.
\]
The exponent is an integer, as the displayed degree formulas show.
After extracting this power, reducing $a_r$ gives $e_r$.
Summing over all choices with the same $\ell$ and $b$ therefore gives
exactly
\[
 [z^bX^\ell]\,
 \overline E(X^{p+1})
 \left(1+z\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}X^{(p+1)p^j-2}\right).
\]
Finally, replacing $a_r$ by an integral lift of $e_r$ introduces a
coefficient divisible by $p$. Its weighted order is at least
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(p)+\frac{2b}{p+1}
 =(p-1)p^{n-1}+\frac{2b}{p+1}>\frac4{p+1}.
\]
Hence coefficient reduction also preserves every contribution below
the cutoff. All discarded terms have weighted order at least
$4/(p+1)$, proving the proposition.
head: environment

label: rem:equal-distance
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:equal-distance}
Every active defect-two Witt level has the same weighted order
$2/(p+1)$. Higher levels therefore do not become individually
negligible. Formula~\eqref{eq:weighted-monomial-order} makes this
fact visible without changing the valuation normalization.
head: environment

label: lem:initial-minor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:initial-minor}
Below height $h(k)+4/(p+1)$, only the principal minor indexed by
$\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}$ can contribute to $b_k(\pi_{\chi_n})$.
Its contributions at relative weighted orders zero and $2/(p+1)$
are recorded by the constant and linear coefficients of
$\det A_{n,\{0,\ldots,k-1\}}(z)$.
head: environment
name: Initial-minor reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
The initial set uniquely minimizes the index sum, at $\binom{k}{2}$.
Every other set has excess at least one, and hence valuation at
least $h(k)+(p-1)/(p+1)\geq h(k)+4/(p+1)$ because $p\geq5$.
At $p=5$ equality is permitted: the statement only concerns heights
strictly below this boundary. The residue dictionary above proves
the final assertion.
head: environment

label: lem:contact-blocks
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Invertibility of contact blocks

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:Hodge-contact} gives
$v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(b_k(\pi_{\chi_n}))=h(k)$.
The initial-minor reduction identifies its leading residue, up
to sign, with the determinant of the leading initial matrix.
That determinant is therefore nonzero. After grouping residues
it is, up to sign, the product of the square block determinants,
so every factor is nonzero. Figure~\ref{fig:contact-block-invertibility}
illustrates the factorization and the block sizes.
head: environment

label: lem:AH-recurrence
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Artin--Hasse coefficient recurrence

title: Proof
body_md:
Differentiating the defining exponent of $E(w)$ gives
\[
 wE'(w)=E(w)\sum_{h\geq0}w^{p^h}.
\]
Both sides have $p$-integral coefficients, so we may reduce modulo $p$.
The coefficient of $w^\nu$ on the left is $\nu e_\nu$, and that on the
right is $\sum_{h\geq0}e_{\nu-p^h}$.  This proves the identity for
$\nu\geq0$.  For $\nu<0$, both sides vanish by convention.
head: environment

label: lem:D-rho
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:D-rho}
The vector $\rho_i$ spans the right nullspace of $\mathbf D_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a row index $0\leq u<p^{i-1}$, the definition of $\rho_i$ gives
\[
 (\mathbf D_i\rho_i)_u
 =e_{pu+p-1}+\sum_{h=0}^{i-1}e_{pu+p-1-p^h}.
\]
The first term comes from column $v=0$, and the sum comes from the
columns $v=p^h$.  Since $pu+p-1\leq p^i-1$, all terms with $h\geq i$
would have negative index and vanish.  The recurrence thus gives
\[
 \sum_{h=0}^{i-1}e_{pu+p-1-p^h}
 =(pu+p-1)e_{pu+p-1}=-e_{pu+p-1}
 \quad\text{in }\mathbf F_p.
\]
Consequently $\mathbf D_i\rho_i=0$.  The vector is nonzero, and the nullspace has
dimension one by \eqref{eq:block-ranks}, so it spans that nullspace.
head: environment

label: prop:shift-register
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Cancellation of older levels and detection of level $i$

label: eq:B-rho
title: Proof
body_md:
First multiply $\mathbf B_{i,j}$ by the explicit vector $\rho_i$.  For
$0\leq u\leq p^{i-1}$,
\[
 (\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i)_u
 =e_{pu+1-p^j}+\sum_{h=0}^{i-1}e_{pu+1-p^j-p^h}.
\]
Here
\[
 pu+1-p^j\leq p^i+1-p^j<p^i,
\]
since $j\geq1$.  Therefore the terms with $h\geq i$ in the
Artin--Hasse recurrence all vanish.  Applying that recurrence yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:B-rho}
 \begin{aligned}
 (\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i)_u
  &=\bigl(pu+2-p^j\bigr)e_{pu+1-p^j}\\
  &=2e_{pu+1-p^j}\quad\text{in }\mathbf F_p.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This also holds when $pu+1-p^j<0$, since then every term is zero.
We now pair the resulting vector with $\lambda_i$.

\paragraph{Older levels: $j<i$.}
The column index $p^j-1$ satisfies
$0\leq p^j-1<p^{i-1}$, so it is a column of $\mathbf C_i$.  Its entry in row $u$
is exactly
\[
 e_{pu-(p^j-1)}=e_{pu+1-p^j}.
\]
Thus $\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i$ is twice this column of $\mathbf C_i$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:lambda} says that pairing any such column with
$\lambda_i$ gives zero.  This proves the first case.

\paragraph{The current level: $j=i$.}
For $u<p^{i-1}$,
\[
 pu+1-p^i\leq1-p<0,
\]
whereas for $u=p^{i-1}$ the index is $1$.  Because $e_1=1$, equation
\eqref{eq:B-rho} therefore gives
\[
 \mathbf B_{i,i}\rho_i=(0,\ldots,0,2)^T.
\]
The last coordinate of $\lambda_i$ is one, so the pairing is $2$.
The matrix itself makes the location of this contribution explicit:
for $i\geq2$,
\[
\mathbf B_{i,i}=\begin{blockarray}{rccccc}
 &v=0&v=1&v=2&\cdots&v=p^{i-1}\\
\begin{block}{r[ccccc]}
 u=0&0&0&0&\cdots&0\\
 \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\
 u=p^{i-1}-1&0&0&0&\cdots&0\\
 \cline{2-6}
 u=p^{i-1}&1&1&0&\cdots&0\\
\end{block}
\end{blockarray}.
\]
Thus its first $p^{i-1}$ rows are zero, and its last row has nonzero
entries only in columns $0$ and $1$.  Both corresponding coordinates of
$\rho_i$ equal one.

\paragraph{Newer levels: $j>i$.}
For every $u\leq p^{i-1}$,
\[
 pu+1-p^j\leq p^i+1-p^{i+1}<0.
\]
Consequently $\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i=0$, proving the last case.
head: environment

label: thm:detector
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Conductor detector

title: Proof
body_md:
The constant term of the initial residue determinant is zero,
because its leading matrix has corank one.
Proposition~\ref{prop:shift-register} gives
\[
 \sum_{1\leq j<n}\lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i
 =\begin{cases}2,&n>i,\\0,&n\leq i.\end{cases}
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:detector-minor} gives a nonzero linear coefficient
precisely when $n>i$: it is twice the nonzero contact determinant.
For $n=1$ the sum is empty, as required.

The residue dictionary in \eqref{eq:minor-factorization} now shows
that the initial principal determinant has valuation exactly
$h(K_i)+2/(p+1)$ when $n>i$, and at least $h(K_i)+4/(p+1)$ otherwise.
In the first case the displayed height is an integer, as it must be:
$K_i\equiv2\pmod{p+1}$ gives
\[
 h(K_i)+\frac2{p+1}
 =\frac{(p-1)K_i(K_i-1)/2+2}{p+1}\in\mathbf Z.
\]
The parameter and coefficient errors lie above the retained precision.
Finally every noninitial Fredholm minor has valuation at least
$h(K_i)+(p-1)/(p+1)\geq h(K_i)+4/(p+1)$.
This is strictly above the active height $h(K_i)+2/(p+1)$,
and at least the claimed inactive lower bound, also when $p=5$.
It cannot cancel the nonzero leading contribution or lower the
bound in the inactive case. This proves both assertions.
head: environment

label: prop:vertex
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Active and inactive Newton heights

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The ramification and genus statements are Proposition~\ref{prop:breaks} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:genus}.  At conductor $p^i$, the $i$-th Artin--Hasse
parameter vanishes by \eqref{eq:pi-specialization}; at conductor $p^{i+1}$ it
is active.  Proposition~\ref{prop:vertex} gives
\[
 N_i(K_i)>h(K_i)+\frac{2}{p+1},
 \qquad
 N_{i+1}(K_i)=h(K_i)+\frac{2}{p+1}.
\]
These inequalities show a \emph{strict downward change} in the polygon
height at $K_i$ when the conductor increases from $p^i$ to $p^{i+1}$.
The newly active $i$-th Witt level creates the nonzero term of weighted excess $2/(p+1)$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:vertex} makes the resulting point
an actual Newton vertex.

For this fixed $i$, the same proposition gives
\[
 N_n(K_i)=h(K_i)+\frac{2}{p+1}
 \qquad\text{for every }n>i.
\]
Thus the height at $K_i$ stabilizes after its drop.  At the next increase
of conductor there is, however, a new drop at $K_{i+1}$, and this happens
for every $i$.  Since $K_i=(p+1)p^{i-1}+2$ tends to infinity, the changes
continue at increasingly large abscissas.  Stabilization at each of these
fixed abscissas therefore coexists with failure of stabilization of the
entire normalized polygon.

These are the same normalized polygons used in
Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence}. For every proposed conductor
threshold, taking $i$ sufficiently large gives two consecutive higher
conductors whose polygons differ at $K_i$.  They are not eventually
independent, and Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence} implies that the tower
is not slope stable.
head: environment

label: prop:complete-not-strong
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:complete-not-strong}
For the tower \eqref{eq:complete-not-strong-tower} over $\mathbf F_5$,
\[
 f=[X]^6+\sum_{j\geq1}5^j[X]^{6\cdot5^j-2},
 \qquad D_n=6\cdot5^{n-1},
\]
one has, for every $r\geq n\geq2$,
\[
 N_r|_{[0,D_n+1]}=N_n|_{[0,D_n+1]}=N_\infty|_{[0,D_n+1]},
 \qquad
 S_r\cap(0,5^{n-r})=5^{n-r}S_n.
\]
Nevertheless $N_n$ and $N_{n+1}$ differ at $D_n+2$, and
\[
 R_n=D_n+1\qquad(n\geq2).
\]
Thus complete first-block propagation holds, but two-block propagation
and full slope stability fail.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The ramification formulas in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} give
$m=0$, $d=\delta=6$, and the displayed $D_n$.
Corollary~\ref{cor:small-degree} proves the initial-polygon criterion.
To make its starting level explicit, recall that the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:all-slope-propagation} requires
\[
 D_n>A,\qquad D_n\geq2A,\qquad n\geq2,\qquad
 (p-2)p^{n-1}>C/\delta.
\]
Here
\[
 A=6\left\lceil\frac{25}{48}\right\rceil=6,
 \qquad C/\delta=\frac{25}{12}.
\]
At $n=2$, these conditions read $30>6$, $30\geq12$, and
$15>25/12$; all remain valid as $n$ increases. That theorem therefore
identifies the polygons through $D_n$ at every higher level. The next
integer, $D_n+1$, is a common contact, so agreement extends through it.
The primitive-slope identity follows by dividing characteristic slopes
at levels $n$ and $r$ by $4\cdot5^{n-1}$ and $4\cdot5^{r-1}$,
respectively. Every element of $5^{n-r}S_n$ is already strictly between
zero and $5^{n-r}$.

At $K_n=D_n+2$, Proposition~\ref{prop:vertex} gives
\[
 N_n(K_n)>h(K_n)+\frac13
       =N_{n+1}(K_n)=N_\infty(K_n).
\]
The last equality follows from the same active-height formula at every
level greater than $n$ and local convergence to $N_\infty$.
All these polygons have integer vertex abscissas, so each is linear on
$[D_n+1,D_n+2]$. Their common left endpoint and different right endpoints
force disagreement at every interior point. This proves $R_n=D_n+1$.
Finally $D_n+2<2D_n$, so the two-block polygon criterion in
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-block-stability} rules out two-block
propagation. Full slope stability is already excluded by
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
head: environment

label: rem:upward-change
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:upward-change}
Over $\mathbf F_7$, consider
\begin{equation}\label{eq:upward-change-tower}
 f=[X]^8+[2][X]^6+\sum_{j\geq1}7^j[X]^{8\cdot7^j-2}.
\end{equation}
It has $D_n=8\cdot7^{n-1}$ and $h(k)=3k(k-1)/8$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:degree-eight-coefficient} verifies the first-block
criterion. Its starting conditions hold at $n=2$: here $A=8$,
$C/\delta=147/32$, $D_2=56\geq2A$, and $5\cdot7>147/32$.
Hence the polygons agree through $D_n+1$ for all higher levels.
At $K_i=D_i+2$, however, the conductor change produces an upward jump.
We give the additional calculation to justify that assertion.

Use the null vectors $\lambda_i,\rho_i$ and bridges $\mathbf B_{i,j}$
of Section~\ref{sec:cofactor-principle}. The added level-zero monomial
has the same excess $1/4$ as the tails. Its bridge, before multiplying
by its coefficient two, is
\[
 \mathbf B_{i,0}=(e_{7u-v})_{0\leq u,v\leq7^{i-1}}.
\]
The support of $\rho_i$ and the Artin--Hasse recurrence give
\[
 (\mathbf B_{i,0}\rho_i)_u
 =e_{7u}+\sum_{b=0}^{i-1}e_{7u-7^b}
 =e_{7u}-\mathbf1_{\{u=7^{i-1}\}}.
\]
Indeed the sum over all $b\geq0$ vanishes; among its omitted terms,
only $b=i$, $u=7^{i-1}$ can contribute. The vector $(e_{7u})_u$
is a column of $\mathbf C_i$, annihilated by $\lambda_i^T$, and
$\lambda_i$ has last coordinate one. Thus
\[
 \lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,0}\rho_i=-1,
 \qquad
 2\lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,0}\rho_i+
 \sum_{1\leq j<n}\lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i
 =-2+2\mathbf1_{\{n>i\}}.
\]
For $i\geq2$, this is nonzero at level $i$ and zero at every higher
level. The residue dictionary therefore gives coefficient heights
$h(K_i)+1/4$ at level $i$ and at least $h(K_i)+1/2$ afterward.
Two tail occurrences cost at least $1/2$, a noninitial minor costs
at least $3/4$, and the parameter and coefficient errors are larger;
thus none interferes with the tested excess $1/4$.
Every chord across the integer $K_i$ has height at least
$h(K_i)+3/8$, by \eqref{eq:chord-identity}. Consequently
\[
 N_i(K_i)=h(K_i)+\frac14,
 \qquad N_n(K_i)\geq h(K_i)+\frac38\quad(n>i).
\]
The same lower bound holds for $N_\infty(K_i)$. This gives an upward
change and again $R_i=D_i+1$ for $i\geq2$. Together with the downward
changes of the preceding family, it shows that no general monotonicity
in the conductor should be imposed on the sequence $N_n$.

label: thm:positive-loss
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:positive-loss}
Consider the $\mathbf Z_7$-tower over $\mathbf F_7$ defined by
\[
 f=[X]^{11}+\sum_{j\geq2}7^j[X]^{11\cdot7^j-19}.
\]
Then $D_n=11\cdot7^{n-1}$ and $h(k)=3k(k-1)/11$.
For every $n\geq2$, at $K=D_n-4$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-witness}
 N_n(K)=h(K)+\frac{72}{11},\qquad
 N_{n+1}(K)\leq h(K)+\frac{61}{11}.
\end{equation}
The same upper bound at $K$ holds for $N_\infty(K)$.
Both $N_{n+1}(x)$ and $N_\infty(x)$ lie strictly below $N_n(x)$
throughout $(D_n-10,D_n)$. Together with the agreement through
$D_n-10$ supplied by Corollary~\ref{cor:degree-eleven-loss}, this gives
\[
 R_n=D_n-10\qquad(n\geq2).
\]
Thus eventual minimal break ratios do not force agreement with
the limit on the entire first characteristic block.

label: lem:loss-square-blocks
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:loss-square-blocks}
For every $t\geq0$ and $0\leq c\leq6$, the square matrix
\[
 (e_{7u-v+c})_{0\leq u,v<t}
\]
is invertible over $\mathbf F_7$. The determinant of the empty
matrix is interpreted as one.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is the contact-block argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:contact-blocks},
now applied to the monomial tower $[X]^{11}$ and residues modulo eleven.
At its contact index $11t$, every noninitial principal minor has strictly
positive excess over the Hodge bound. Thus the leading initial matrix
has nonzero determinant modulo seven. Group rows by a residue
$a\in\{0,\ldots,10\}$ and pair them with columns of residue
$7a\bmod11$, represented in $\{0,\ldots,10\}$. Its square blocks are
\[
 (e_{7u-v+\lfloor7a/11\rfloor})_{0\leq u,v<t}.
\]
Their determinant product, up to sign, is nonzero. The shifts
$\lfloor7a/11\rfloor$ run through $0,\ldots,6$, so every stated
matrix is invertible. These are also the matrices occurring among the
contact blocks in the characteristic-seven case of
Lemma~\ref{lem:contact-blocks};
only their grouping by residues has changed.

label: lem:degree-eleven-monomial
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}
For the monomial tower $[X]^{11}$ over $\mathbf F_7$, every classical
characteristic polygon, and its reduced limiting polygon, is the Hodge
contact polygon for $h(k)=3k(k-1)/11$. Its slopes are
\[
 \bigsqcup_{j\geq0}
 \{6j,\ \underbrace{6j+3,\ldots,6j+3}_{10\text{ times}}\}.
\]
In particular its segment on $[1,11]$ is $y=3(x-1)$, and its
maximum excess above $h$ is $75/11$.
head: environment
name: The degree-eleven monomial polygon

label: eq:loss-residue-cycle
title: Proof
body_md:
The entry with original
row and column indices $u,v$ in its leading residue matrix is
$e_{(7u-v)/11}$ if $v\equiv7u\pmod{11}$, and is zero otherwise.
Thus a row of residue $a$ can meet only a column of residue $7a$.
Multiplication by seven has the single cycle
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-residue-cycle}
 1\longmapsto7\longmapsto5\longmapsto2\longmapsto3
 \longmapsto10\longmapsto4\longmapsto6\longmapsto9
 \longmapsto8\longmapsto1
\end{equation}
on the ten nonzero residues modulo eleven.

Let $I$ be the common row and column index set of a principal submatrix.
If its determinant is nonzero, some permutation term is nonzero. That
term matches every selected row to a distinct selected column, with a row
of residue $a$ matched to a column of residue $7a$. Consequently
\[
 \#\{u\in I:u\equiv a\pmod{11}\}
 =\#\{u\in I:u\equiv7a\pmod{11}\}.
\]
Following the cycle shows that all ten nonzero residue classes have the
same count. The zero-residue count can be different.

The same residue restriction holds before reduction: the splitting
series is $E(\pi_0(T)X^{11})$, so its coefficients vanish in degrees
not divisible by eleven. For either a classical specialization or the
reduced universal series, every nonzero determinant term has valuation
at least $\frac6{11}\sum_{u\in I}u$.
For a classical character of order $7^r$, an integral coefficient
divisible by seven contributes an additional valuation of at least
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(7)=\varphi(7^r)=6\cdot7^{r-1}.
\]
Indeed $v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_r}))=1$, so
$\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_r})^m a$ with $a\in7\mathbf Z_7$ has valuation
at least $m+6\cdot7^{r-1}$. Such coefficients vanish in the reduced
series, and at classical characters only increase the lower bound.
Thus it suffices to bound the index sum, without assuming that every
Artin--Hasse coefficient is a unit.

Denote the common count in each nonzero residue class by $t$, and let $z$
be the number of selected indices divisible by eleven. Thus the size is
$k=z+10t$. The smallest possible index sum is
\[
 \sum_{v=0}^{z-1}11v+
 \sum_{b=1}^{10}\sum_{v=0}^{t-1}(11v+b)
 =\frac{11z(z-1)}2+55t^2.
\]
Multiplying by $6/11$ and subtracting $h(k)$ gives
\[
 3z(z-1)+30t^2-h(z+10t)
 =\frac{30(z-t)(z-t-1)}{11}.
\]
The difference $z-t$ is congruent to $k$ modulo eleven.
For example, when $k=10$, the choice $t=1$, $z=0$ has minimum
index sum $1+\cdots+10=55$ and hence valuation at least
$(6/11)\cdot55=30>3(10-1)$. The alternative $t=0$, $z=10$
has an even larger lower bound. The following comparison treats every
size at once.

To compare this with the contact polygon, write $k=11j+r$ with
$1\leq r\leq11$. The contact chord from $11j+1$ to $11j+11$ has
excess over $h(k)$ equal to
\[
 \frac3{11}(r-1)(11-r).
\]
Among all integers congruent to $r$ modulo eleven, the quadratic
$u(u-1)$ is minimized at one of $u=r$ and $u=r-11$.
For these two possibilities the desired comparison follows from
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 30r(r-1)-3(r-1)(11-r)&=33(r-1)^2\geq0,\\
 30(r-11)(r-12)-3(r-1)(11-r)&=33(11-r)^2\geq0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus every coefficient point lies on or above the contact chord.
The possible restriction $z,t\geq0$ only increases this lower bound.
The common contacts at $k\equiv0,1\pmod{11}$, including the initial
contact at zero, force equality with the contact polygon.

The segment from $11j$ to $11j+1$ has slope
$h(11j+1)-h(11j)=6j$ and length one. The next segment, from $11j+1$
to $11j+11$, has slope $6j+3$ and length ten. This proves the
stated slope list.
Its maximum excess over $h$ is $75/11$.

The contact equalities used here hold for every classical conductor
and for the reduced limiting polygon. The argument therefore proves
both assertions at once.

label: lem:loss-first-block
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}, the monomial polygon
on $[1,11]$ is the chord $y=3(x-1)$, whose excess above $h$ is
\[
 3(k-1)-h(k)=\frac3{11}(k-1)(11-k)\leq\frac{75}{11}.
\]
We next restore the higher Witt terms of the tower in
Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss}. They all have level at least two, so
$f^{<2}=[X]^{11}$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tail-estimate} with truncation
level two and arbitrary character level $r\geq2$. Since
$p=7$, $\delta=11$, and $D_2=77$, it gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}\bigl(b_k(f,\pi_{\chi_r})-b_k([X]^{11},\pi_{\chi_r})\bigr)
 \geq h(k)+\frac{6(77-k+1)+1}{11}.
\]
For $1\leq k\leq11$, the added quantity is at least $403/11$, which
is strictly larger than the maximum chord excess $75/11$. Hence every
coefficient perturbation lies strictly above $3(k-1)$. The original
coefficient points on or above the chord remain on or above it. At
$k=1,11$, the perturbation has strictly higher valuation and preserves
the contact height. Taking the lower convex hull therefore preserves
the whole segment. This proves $N_r(x)=3(x-1)$ on $[1,11]$.

Finally, the reflected-excess identity \eqref{eq:reflected-excess} says
\[
 N_n(k)-h(k)=N_n(D_n-k+1)-h(D_n-k+1).
\]
It expresses slope symmetry after accounting for the initial zero slope
of the characteristic series. At $K=D_n-4$, the reflected index is
$D_n-K+1=5$. Since $N_n(5)=12$ and $h(5)=60/11$, we obtain
\[
 N_n(K)-h(K)=N_n(5)-h(5)=12-\frac{60}{11}=\frac{72}{11}.
\]
Reflection sends $[1,11]$ to $[D_n-10,D_n]$. Substitution throughout
that interval gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 N_n(x)&=h(x)-h(D_n-x+1)+3(D_n-x)\\
 &=h(D_n)+\left(\frac{6D_n}{11}-3\right)(x-D_n).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The expression is linear. The identity at integer points extends across
the interval because Newton polygon vertices have integer abscissas.
This proves the last assertion.

label: lem:loss-index-set
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The index set for one new term

title: Proof
body_md:
A term linear in $z$ selects one new entry and otherwise uses entries
from $\overline E(X^{11})$. Suppose the new entry has row residue $a$
and column residue $c$. Since $\ell\equiv-19\pmod{11}$,
\[
 c\equiv7a-\ell\equiv7a+8\pmod{11}.
\]
Every other selected entry sends a row residue $b$ to column residue $7b$.
We first determine which counts of indices can support such a permutation.

Write $m_b$ for the number of indices of $I$ of residue $b$.
After deleting the row and column occupied by the new entry, the remaining
matching requires
\[
 m_{7b}-\mathbf1_{\{7b=c\}}
 =m_b-\mathbf1_{\{b=a\}}\qquad(b\bmod11).
\]
At $b=0$, this excludes exactly one of $a,c$ being zero; they cannot both
be zero because $c=7a+8$. Thus both are nonzero. Along the cycle
\eqref{eq:loss-residue-cycle}, the count increases by one on entering $c$
and decreases by one on leaving $a$. It is constant elsewhere.
Hence the larger counts form the consecutive arc starting at $c$ and
ending at $a$, both endpoints included. Counts on this arc exceed those
off the arc by one.

We next restrict the zero-residue count. The initial set
$\{0,\ldots,K-1\}$ contains $L$ multiples of eleven.
To have at least $L+2$ such multiples, a set must add at least
$11L$ and $11L+11$ and remove two nonzero-residue indices no larger
than $11L-5$ and $11L-6$. Its index excess is therefore at least
\[
 11L+(11L+11)-(11L-5)-(11L-6)=22.
\]
To have at most $L-2$ multiples of eleven, it must remove two such
indices no larger than $11L-11$ and $11L-22$, while the smallest
available new nonzero indices are $11L-4$ and $11L-3$.
The excess is then at least
\[
 (11L-4)+(11L-3)-(11L-11)-(11L-22)=26.
\]
Every further replacement increases the sum. At excess at most seven,
we can therefore write $m_0=L+s$ with $s\in\{-1,0,1\}$.

There remain $10L-4-s$ nonzero indices. If the smaller nonzero count
is $t$ and the arc has length $a_0$, then
$10t+a_0=10L-4-s$, with $1\leq a_0\leq9$.
It follows that $t=L-1$ and $a_0=6-s$. Thus the larger count is $L$,
and the only possible arc lengths are five, six, and seven.

For fixed residue counts, the smallest index sum is obtained by taking
the smallest available indices in each residue class. The zero class
contributes $11(L+s)(L+s-1)/2$. Taking $L-1$ indices in each nonzero
class contributes
\[
 \sum_{b=1}^{10}\sum_{v=0}^{L-2}(11v+b)=55(L-1)^2.
\]
For each residue on the larger-count arc, one adds the index
$11(L-1)+b$. Subtracting the initial index sum gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-prefix-excess}
\begin{aligned}
 E_{\min}
 &=\frac{11}{2}(L+s)(L+s-1)+55(L-1)^2
   +11(L-1)(6-s)\\
 &\hspace{1.5em}+\sum_{b\text{ on the arc}}b
   -\frac{(11L-4)(11L-5)}2\\
 &=\sum_{b\text{ on the arc}}b-21+\frac{11}{2}s(s+1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In particular the dependence on $L$ cancels.

For completeness, the allowed new row residues
$a=1,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10$ give arc lengths
$5,4,3,8,1,9,2,7,6$, respectively. The row residue $2$ is excluded
because its new column has residue zero. Keeping only lengths five,
six, and seven leaves the following three possibilities:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccl@{}}
\toprule
New row & New column & $s$ & $E_{\min}$ & Larger-count arc\\
\midrule
$1$ & $4$ & $1$ & $18$ & $4,6,9,8,1$\\
$9$ & $5$ & $-1$ & $18$ & $5,2,3,10,4,6,9$\\
$10$ & $1$ & $0$ & $7$ & $1,7,5,2,3,10$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For example, the last arc has residue sum $28$, giving $28-21=7$.
Changing any initial segment within a fixed residue class raises the
index sum by at least eleven. Therefore only the last row of the table,
with the smallest indices in each class, can occur at excess at most
seven. Those indices are exactly \eqref{eq:loss-index-set}.
Relative to $\{0,\ldots,11L-5\}$, this set removes
$11L-7,11L-5$ and adds $11L-4,11L-1$, for a net excess of seven.

body_md:

If the first-block multiset identity held, Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-block-stability}

propagation fails.

label: thm:annular-failure
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Failure of a uniform annular slope law

label: lem:annular-monomial
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:annular-monomial}
For the tower \eqref{eq:annular-witt-vector}, every classical
characteristic polygon and the limiting polygon equal the monomial
polygon of Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}. Their slopes are
\eqref{eq:annular-limit-slopes}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The monomial polygon has maximum excess $75/11$ over $h$.
In the reduced universal series, a tail monomial at level $n_r$ has
weighted order
\[
 7^{n_r}-\frac{11\cdot7^{n_r}-96}{11}=\frac{96}{11}.
\]
Every term in the difference of a full Fredholm coefficient and its
monomial counterpart uses at least one tail occurrence. Its principal
index sum contributes at least $h(k)$, so the difference has valuation
at least $h(k)+96/11$, strictly above the monomial polygon.
Its contact vertices are therefore preserved, and no other coefficient
point can fall below it. This proves equality of the limiting polygons.

At a finite character of order $7^m$, each active tail has level
$n_r<m$ and parameter valuation $7^{n_r}$; inactive tails vanish.
The weighted order of each active tail is again $96/11$.
The same coefficient comparison preserves the entire monomial polygon
at every conductor. Thus every normalized classical polygon equals
the limiting polygon, and Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence}
gives slope stability.
head: environment

label: lem:annular-effective-gap
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:annular-effective-gap}
At this weight,
\[
 v_{T_0}\left(\frac{\pi_i(T_0)}{\pi_0(T_0)^{7^i}}-1\right)
 \geq\frac{318}{11}\quad(0\leq i<n),
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-new-parameter}
 v_{T_0}\left(\frac{\pi_n(T_0)}{7\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}}-1\right)
 \geq\frac{77}{11}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $\ell=11\cdot7^n-96$,
\[
 v_{T_0}(\pi_n(T_0))-\frac\ell{11}=\frac{18}{11}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Evaluate the formal congruence
$\pi_i(T)-\pi_0(T)^{7^i}\in7T\mathbf Z_7[[T]]$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi-congruence} at $T=T_0$, and divide by
$\pi_0(T_0)^{7^i}$. For $i<n$ this gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 v_{T_0}\left(\frac{\pi_i(T_0)}{\pi_0(T_0)^{7^i}}-1\right)
 &\geq v_{T_0}(7)+1-7^i\\
 &\geq\frac{6(D_n-13)+11-D_n}{11}
 =\frac{5D_n-67}{11}\geq\frac{318}{11},
 \end{aligned}
\]
since $D_n\geq77$. For $i=0$ the difference is zero and its valuation
is infinite. In particular $\pi_{n-1}(T_0)$ has valuation $D_n/11$,
and its ratio to $\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}$ is one to the stated precision.

Put $y(T_0)=E(\pi_{n-1}(T_0))-1$. The defining identities give
\[
 E(\pi_n(T_0))-1=(1+y(T_0))^7-1
 =7y(T_0)+\sum_{j=2}^{6}\binom7j y(T_0)^j+y(T_0)^7.
\]
Here $v_{T_0}(y(T_0))=D_n/11$, because
$E(U)-1=U+O(U^2)$ preserves positive valuations and
$v_{T_0}(\pi_{n-1}(T_0))=D_n/11$.
The first term has valuation
\[
 v_{T_0}(7y(T_0))=\frac{6(D_n-13)+D_n}{11}
 =\frac{7D_n-78}{11}.
\]
For $2\leq j\leq6$, the coefficient $\binom7j$ has seven-adic
valuation one, so its term is higher than $7y(T_0)$ by
$(j-1)D_n/11\geq77/11$. The last term is higher by
\[
 v_{T_0}(y(T_0)^7)-v_{T_0}(7y(T_0))=\frac{78}{11}.
\]
Also, replacing $y(T_0)$ by $\pi_{n-1}(T_0)$ in $7y(T_0)$ introduces a relative error of
valuation at least $D_n/11\geq77/11$.

Applying \eqref{eq:pi-first-two-terms} at $j=n$ and $T=T_0$ gives
\[
 \pi_n(T_0)=(1+T_0)^{7^n}-1
       +O\!\left(\bigl((1+T_0)^{7^n}-1\bigr)^2\right).
\]
This inverse substitution introduces a relative error of valuation
at least $v_{T_0}((1+T_0)^{7^n}-1)=(7D_n-78)/11>77/11$.
Combining these estimates, and finally replacing $\pi_{n-1}(T_0)$ by
$\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}$, proves \eqref{eq:annular-new-parameter}.
The leading term is consequently $7\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}$, with valuation
$(7D_n-78)/11$. Subtracting $\ell/11=(7D_n-96)/11$ gives $18/11$.
